title: ASSOCIATIONS BETWEEN URBAN SOUNDSCAPE PERCEPTION AND EMOTIONAL STATES
authors: Maria Luiza de Ulhôa Carvalho et al., 2023
research_question: How can real-time EEG measurements be compatible with VR method in urban soundscape studies? How to overcome electric line noise in EEG data originated from VR HMD? How does different human occupancy and nature sound in different urban scenarios effect EEG alpha power? Can higher educated individuals differ in brain activity when assessing urban soundscapes through VR? Can the university community identify places that represent the ISO’s 4 PAQs quadrants? Can the number of people shift ISO’s PAQ responses in different urban areas? Can children’s sounds induce vibrancy?

participants.description: Experiment 1: 23 members (67% men, 33% women) of the School of Science, Engineering & Environment, University of Salford. Experiment 2: 50 participants (30 at library: 55% men, 45% women; 20 at park: 60% men, 40% women). Experiment 3: 11 participants (36% men, 64% women, average age 28±8). Experiment 4: 155 participants from 63 countries (Group 1: 75 individuals, 49% women, 48% males, 3% non-binary, age 21-68, mean 38±12; Group 2: 80 individuals, 51% women, 45% males, 4% non-binary, age 21-67, mean 38±11). Experiment 5: 36 participants (64% men, 36% women, average age 32±10) from 11 countries (47% UK, 17% India, 6% Brazil, Chile, China, Poland, 3% Ecuador, Egypt, Iran, Myanmar, Pakistan). Educational levels varied, with 86% having level 6 or more in Exp 5. Acoustic/musical background varied.
participants.recruitment: Experiment 1: Randomly approached students and staff. Experiment 2: Randomly approached local experts. Experiment 3: Randomly approached attendees at a public academic event. Experiment 4: Social media advertisement, mailing lists, online social networks. Experiment 5: Mailing list of Acoustic Research Centre of Salford.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Open questions asking for public spaces representing soundscape categories (Exciting, Calm, Chaotic, Monotonous).
Peel Park (nature sounds, people talking, children playing) and Clifford Whitworth Library (people talking softly, typing).
30-second 360° audio-visual samples of Piccadilly Gardens at empty, medium, and busy population densities. Audio in B-format.
1-minute 360° audio-visual samples of Piccadilly Gardens (Plaza), Market Street (Street), a bus stop, and Peel Park (Park) at empty, medium, and busy population densities. Spatial audio (ambiX).
8-second 4K resolution 360° audio-visual samples of Piccadilly Gardens (Plaza), Market Street (Street), and Peel Park (Park) at empty and busy population densities. Spatial audio.

measures.instrument: PANAS (Positive and Negative Affect Schedule) - 10 words
ISO’s Perceived Affective Qualities (PAQs: Pleasant to Unpleasant, Eventful to Uneventful, Vibrant to Monotonous, Calm to Chaotic)
SAM (Self-Assessment Manikins) for Valence, Arousal, Dominance
Plutchik’s wheel of emotions (32 emotional options)
Sound levels (SPL), Loudness, Sharpness, Roughness, Fluctuation Strength, Tonality, Tonality Threshold

findings.consequent: EEG Alpha Power at occipital regions
findings.mechanism: alpha brain waves can be induced at the posterior brain regions by relaxation and drowsiness (Teplan, 2002), the increased values of alpha power at occipital regions in empty locations may indicate participants were more relaxed when there were no people in the scene.
findings.quote: EEG alpha power results demonstrated a significant effect of population density when data was clustered. Considering alpha brain waves can be induced at the posterior brain regions by relaxation and drowsiness (Teplan, 2002), the increased values of alpha power at occipital regions in empty locations may indicate participants were more relaxed when there were no people in the scene.

findings.consequent: significant differences in EEG alpha power across brain regions due to population density
findings.mechanism: This result may indicate an effect of educational level on EEG responses of participants with higher education demonstrating more consensus in brain activity than those with lower education level.
findings.quote: Another interesting finding was that participants from EEG cluster 2 were predominantly highly educated individuals, and eight out of 10 brain regions had significant differences in population density conditions, whilst cluster 1 had only three regions significantly different.

mechanisms: Natural sounds in parks contribute to stress recovery.
Academic environments can induce tension and determination.
Population density influences soundscape perception and emotional responses, particularly eventfulness and vibrancy.
Cultural differences, including language translation and cultural hegemony, can affect subjective perception and emotional ratings of soundscapes.
Alpha brain waves in posterior brain regions are associated with relaxation and drowsiness, suggesting that empty locations with natural sounds promote relaxation.
Higher educational levels may lead to more consistent EEG responses to environmental stimuli, possibly indicating a more consensual brain activity pattern.
implementation_implications: Population density should be considered when assessing, planning, and designing urban soundscapes.
Busy plazas, especially those with children playing and water features, should be integrated into urban soundscape interventions alongside empty parks to promote well-being and vibrancy.
Water features in urban plazas should be preserved to enhance positive soundscapes.
Further research is needed to validate if children's sounds are a key influencing factor in characterizing vibrant soundscapes.
Continued efforts are needed to enhance the translation and validation of soundscape perceptual attributes across different languages and cultures.

limitations: Difficulty in obtaining formal authorization for recordings at certain locations (Train Station, Arndale Shopping Centre).
Uncontrolled experimental environment, small sample size, and interfering noises in the VR pilot experiment.
Uncalibrated audio samples in the VR pilot experiment led to skewed results.
Weak responses from the PANAS questionnaire in the VR pilot experiment.
Challenges in online experiments include lack of controlled laboratory conditions (audio/video reproduction systems), efficient acoustic settings, and consistent researcher-participant contact.
Poor video resolution in earlier VR recordings.
Difficulty in obtaining 'busy' population density conditions for some locations during COVID-19 field recordings.
Long experimental duration for EEG sessions (2.5 hours) was exhausting for participants.
Low absolute power in the Gamma band led to its exclusion from EEG analysis.
Variability in EEG results and different cluster groupings per condition complicated comparative analysis.
Some participants reported difficulty switching emotions, mental effort, tiredness, and external worries during EEG sessions, potentially compromising data quality.

Visual cues in VR HMDs, processed in occipital regions, might confound the interpretation of increased alpha power in these regions, making it difficult to solely attribute it to soundscape audio-visual stimuli.
Auditory masking effects may have limited the identification of more sound sources from audios.
Psychoacoustic metrics were derived from a single stimulus recording per condition, limiting generalizability.
The sampled population (WEIRD group) may not be representative of the global population, limiting the generalizability of findings, especially regarding educational level effects on EEG.
